title: The application/json Media Type for JavaScript Object Notation (JSON)
summary: Registers the application/json media type for JSON, a lightweight text-based, language-independent data interchange format derived from ECMAScript. It is informational and has been replaced by RFC 7159.

eli5.summary: JSON is a simple way to write down data that nearly every program can read. This gave it an official file label.

questions: what is the application/json media type
how do i escape special characters in json
subtitle: Registers the application/json media type for JavaScript Object Notation.

tldr.problem: JSON is a widely-used data format derived from JavaScript, but it lacked an official MIME media type for email and web applications.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4627 formally registers 'application/json' as the media type for JSON, specifies the JSON grammar and encoding rules, and documents how JSON generators and parsers must behave.
tldr.outcome: JSON became the standard data interchange format for web APIs and applications. RFC 7159 later updated this specification with clarifications.

today: RFC 4627 is informational. RFC 7159 updated the JSON specification with additional clarifications and became the newer reference for application/json.

sections.title: What Is JSON
sections.content:
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based, language-independent data interchange format. It is derived from the object literals of JavaScript as defined in the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard.

JSON can represent four primitive types: strings (sequences of Unicode characters), numbers, booleans (true and false), and null. It also has two structured types: objects (unordered collections of name/value pairs where names are strings and values can be any JSON type) and arrays (ordered sequences of zero or more values).

The design goals for JSON were to be minimal (with a small set of formatting rules), portable (language-independent), textual (human-readable), and a subset of JavaScript (so JSON can be safely parsed with JavaScript's eval() function).
sections.eli5: JSON is a simple format that describes data using curly brackets for containers and square brackets for lists. It can store text, numbers, true/false, and null (empty).

sections.title: JSON Grammar and Syntax
sections.content:
A JSON text is a sequence of tokens consisting of six structural characters, strings, numbers, and three literal names. JSON data must be either a serialized object or an array.

The six structural characters are: [ (begin array), ] (end array), { (begin object), } (end object), : (name separator), and , (value separator). Whitespace (space, tab, line feed, and carriage return) is allowed before or after these characters.

A value must be either an object, array, number, string, or one of three literal names: false, null, or true (always lowercase). An object is surrounded by curly brackets and contains zero or more name/value pairs separated by commas. An array is surrounded by square brackets and contains zero or more values separated by commas.

Numbers consist of an optional minus sign, an integer component, an optional fraction part (decimal point followed by digits), and an optional exponent part. Octal and hexadecimal forms, leading zeros, and special values like Infinity or NaN are not permitted.
sections.eli5: JSON uses curly brackets for objects, square brackets for arrays, and colons to separate a name from a value. Numbers, text, true/false, and null are the simple values you can store.

sections.title: Strings and Character Encoding
sections.content:
A string in JSON is a sequence of zero or more Unicode characters enclosed in quotation marks. Characters that must be escaped are: the quotation mark, reverse solidus (backslash), and control characters (U+0000 through U+001F).

Any character may be escaped using a backslash followed by specific codes: \" for quotation mark, \\ for backslash, \/ for solidus, \b for backspace, \f for form feed, \n for line feed, \r for carriage return, \t for tab, or \u followed by four hexadecimal digits for other Unicode characters.

JSON text MUST be encoded in Unicode with UTF-8 as the default encoding. The RFC provides a method to detect whether an octet stream uses UTF-8, UTF-16 (big-endian or little-endian), or UTF-32 (big-endian or little-endian) by examining the pattern of null bytes in the first four octets.
sections.eli5: JSON uses backslash escape codes to include special characters in text, like \n for a line break or \" for a quote mark. JSON is always Unicode text, usually in UTF-8 format.

sections.title: Parsers and Generators
sections.content:
A JSON parser transforms a JSON text into another representation. A compliant parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar. A parser may accept non-JSON forms or extensions, and it may set limits on the size of texts, the maximum depth of nesting, the range of numbers, and the length and character contents of strings.

A JSON generator produces JSON text. The resulting text MUST strictly conform to the JSON grammar. Generators are responsible for ensuring syntactically correct output.
sections.eli5: A parser is a program that reads JSON and turns it into something the program can use. A generator is a program that creates JSON.

sections.title: MIME Media Type Registration
sections.content:
The MIME media type for JSON is application/json. The type name is 'application' and the subtype is 'json'. There are no required or optional parameters.

JSON encoding considerations depend on the Unicode encoding used: JSON is 8-bit compatible when written in UTF-8, but when using UTF-16 or UTF-32, the binary content-transfer-encoding must be used.

The specification notes that JSON applications include ActionScript, C, C#, ColdFusion, Common Lisp, E, Erlang, Java, JavaScript, Lua, Objective CAML, Perl, PHP, Python, Rebol, Ruby, and Scheme.
sections.eli5: application/json is the official label that tells email systems and web browsers that a file contains JSON data. Files can use the .json extension.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes general security issues with scripting languages. JSON is a subset of JavaScript, but a safe subset that excludes assignment and invocation, preventing malicious code execution.

A JSON text can be safely processed by JavaScript's eval() function (which compiles and executes a string) if all non-string characters are valid JSON tokens. The RFC provides a verification method using regular expressions: the implementation tests against forbidden characters, removes legitimate string content, and safely evaluates the result.
sections.eli5: JSON is safe to process through JavaScript because it doesn't allow code execution like regular JavaScript does. Special characters in text are protected with backslash escapes.
